presentingComplaint: Three weeks of progressively worsening headache and low-grade fever, referred back after being discharged 8 days earlier with a diagnosis of 'viral meningitis' when a lumbar puncture showed a lymphocytic CSF.
history: A 41-year-old man, non-diabetic, HIV-negative, presented with a 3-week history of dull global headache, intermittent low-grade evening fever, nausea and reduced appetite. He was seen 10 days ago at another hospital where an LP reportedly showed 'lymphocytes, mildly high protein', bacterial and viral studies were sent, empirical aciclovir was given for 3 days and he was discharged as presumed aseptic/viral meningitis with symptomatic treatment. Instead of resolving in the expected 7-10 days, over the last week he has become steadily drowsier, developed horizontal double vision and one episode of vomiting, prompting re-referral. He reports 4 kg weight loss over two months and drenching night sweats. His mother was treated for pulmonary TB two years ago. No rash, no seizures, no recent travel, no injection drug use, no immunosuppressive therapy.
examination: Ill-looking, mildly dehydrated. Drowsy but rousable and oriented (GCS 14, E3V5M6). Neck stiffness present with positive Kernig sign. Right lateral rectus palsy causing horizontal diplopia (VIth cranial nerve). No papilloedema on fundoscopy; no focal limb weakness; plantars flexor. No skin rash or petechiae. No lymphadenopathy palpable; chest clear; abdomen soft, no organomegaly.
imaging: Contrast MRI brain: basal meningeal enhancement most marked around the interpeduncular and suprasellar cisterns, with early communicating hydrocephalus and a few small enhancing granulomas; no ring-enhancing pyogenic abscess and no temporal-lobe restricted diffusion. Chest X-ray shows subtle upper-zone reticulonodular shadowing.
microbiology: CSF Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra: Mycobacterium tuberculosis detected, rifampicin resistance not detected. CSF AFB smear negative; mycobacterial (MGIT) culture pending. Blood and CSF bacterial cultures sterile at 48h; HSV CSF PCR negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Viral (aseptic) meningitis - the label the patient was given, but the subacute >2-week course, falling CSF glucose, very high protein, basal enhancement and cranial nerve palsy argue strongly against a self-limiting viral process
Partially treated bacterial meningitis - excluded by sterile cultures, negative Gram stain, indolent multi-week course and lymphocytic (not neutrophilic) CSF
Viral encephalitis (HSV) - no seizures, no temporal-lobe changes, HSV PCR negative
Cryptococcal meningitis - HIV-negative, cryptococcal antigen negative
finalDiagnosis: CNS tuberculosis - tuberculous meningitis (basal meningitis with early hydrocephalus and VIth nerve palsy), Xpert Ultra confirmed, initially mislabelled as viral meningitis
citations: British Infection Society - Tuberculous Meningitis (Diagnosis and Treatment) - 2009
WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis: Drug-Susceptible TB and Patient Care - 2022
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Tuberculosis (CNS involvement)
stewardship: Start empirical anti-tubercular therapy without waiting for culture once CSF Xpert Ultra is positive: 4-drug intensive phase (isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol) with adjunctive dexamethasone tapered over 6-8 weeks; add pyridoxine. CNS TB requires a prolonged regimen (typically 9-12 months total). This is directed antimycobacterial therapy, not broad-spectrum empiric antibacterials.
contraindications: Avoid ethambutol dosing without baseline visual acuity/colour-vision check and renal-adjusted dosing
Monitor for isoniazid/rifampicin/pyrazinamide hepatotoxicity (baseline and serial LFTs)
Do not withhold corticosteroids in confirmed TBM - adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality
edgeCases: A lymphocytic CSF wrongly labelled 'viral' that fails to resolve in 7-10 days should trigger reassessment for TBM, especially with falling glucose and rising protein
CSF ADA and AFB smear are frequently negative in TBM and do not exclude it; Xpert Ultra positivity is confirmatory but a negative test still does not rule it out
Hyponatraemia (SIADH/cerebral salt wasting) is common and supports the diagnosis
Early communicating hydrocephalus may need CSF diversion
expectedMaiK: Recognise subacute lymphocytic basal meningitis with cranial nerve palsy as tuberculous meningitis (not viral); send CSF Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and mycobacterial culture and start 4-drug ATT plus adjunctive dexamethasone promptly.
expectedNextQuestions: Duration and tempo of headache/fever and whether symptoms improved or worsened after the presumed viral diagnosis
TB contact history and constitutional symptoms (night sweats, weight loss)
Diplopia, drowsiness or other evolving neurological deficits
expectedInvestigations: Lumbar puncture with paired CSF:serum glucose, protein, cell count and differential
CSF Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra plus AFB smear and mycobacterial culture
Contrast MRI brain (basal enhancement, hydrocephalus, tuberculomas)
HIV test, chest X-ray, serum sodium
